_link.title: I can explain why no magnetic force acts on a wire when it is parallel to the magnetic field

toLevel2.question: What is the magnetic force on a current-carrying wire when the current is parallel to the magnetic field?
toLevel2.correct: Zero — no magnetic force acts on the wire
toLevel2.correctExplanation: When the current direction is parallel to the field, the cross product is zero and no magnetic force is produced.

distractors.answer: Maximum — the force is strongest in this orientation
distractors.explanation: Maximum force occurs when the current is perpendicular to the field, not parallel.

distractors.answer: Half the maximum force on the current-carrying wire
distractors.explanation: The force is exactly zero when parallel, not half the maximum.

distractors.answer: The same as when the wire is perpendicular to it
distractors.explanation: Perpendicular gives maximum force; parallel gives zero force.

toLevel2.question: At what angle between the current and the magnetic field is the force on the wire at its maximum?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The force is given by F = nIlBsinθ. At θ = 90°, sinθ = 1, giving the maximum force.

distractors.answer: 0° (parallel to the field)
distractors.explanation: At 0°, sinθ = 0, giving zero force, not maximum.

distractors.answer: 180° (antiparallel to the field)
distractors.explanation: At 180°, sinθ = 0, giving zero force, not maximum.

distractors.answer: 45° (diagonal to the field)
distractors.explanation: At 45°, sinθ ≈ 0.71, which is less than maximum; maximum is at 90°.

toLevel2.question: A wire carries current northward in a magnetic field also directed northward. What force does the wire experience?
toLevel2.correct: No force, because the current and field are parallel
toLevel2.correctExplanation: When the current and field are in the same direction (parallel), the magnetic force is zero.

distractors.answer: A force directed upward out of the ground surface
distractors.explanation: The force is zero because the current is parallel to the field.

distractors.answer: A force directed toward the east perpendicular to both
distractors.explanation: No force is produced when current and field are parallel.

distractors.answer: A force directed southward opposite to the current flow
distractors.explanation: No force acts when current is parallel to the field.

toLevel2.question: Which orientation of a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field produces zero force?
toLevel2.correct: When the wire runs along the field lines
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Running along the field lines means the current is parallel to the field, giving sinθ = 0 and therefore zero force.

distractors.answer: When the wire is perpendicular to the field lines
distractors.explanation: Perpendicular gives maximum force, not zero.

distractors.answer: When the wire is at 45° to the field lines
distractors.explanation: At 45° the force is non-zero; zero occurs only when parallel.

distractors.answer: When the wire is at any angle to the field lines
distractors.explanation: Zero force occurs specifically at 0° or 180°, not at any angle.

toLevel2.question: A wire carries current antiparallel (opposite direction) to the magnetic field. What is the magnetic force on the wire?
toLevel2.correct: Zero, because antiparallel is still 0° in terms of the cross product magnitude
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Antiparallel means θ = 180°, and sin180° = 0. The force is zero just as it is when the wire is parallel.

distractors.answer: Maximum, because the current opposes the field direction fully
distractors.explanation: Opposing the field at 180° still gives sinθ = 0; maximum is at 90°.

distractors.answer: Double the maximum, because opposition doubles the interaction
distractors.explanation: At 180°, sinθ = 0; the force is zero, not doubled.

distractors.answer: Half the maximum force on the current-carrying wire
distractors.explanation: The force is exactly zero at 180°, not half the maximum.

toLevel2.question: A current-carrying wire parallel to a magnetic field experiences no magnetic force.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: When the current direction is parallel to the field, the cross product is zero and no force is produced.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Students may think current in a field always produces a force, but the angle matters; parallel gives zero.

toLevel2.question: The magnetic force on a wire is maximum when the current is perpendicular to the field.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: At 90°, sinθ = 1, giving the maximum possible force F = nIlB.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Maximum force occurs at 90° (perpendicular) because sin90° = 1.

toLevel2.question: When the current is {{blank:1}} to the magnetic field, the force on the wire is {{blank:2}}.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Parallel current and field give sinθ = 0, resulting in zero magnetic force.

blank:1.explanation: Perpendicular gives maximum force, not zero.
Diagonal gives a non-zero force; zero occurs only when parallel.

blank:2.explanation: Maximum force occurs at perpendicular; parallel gives zero.
The force is zero when parallel, not doubled.

toLevel2.question: To produce the maximum force, the wire must be rotated so the current is {{blank:1}} to the field, at an angle of {{blank:2}} degrees.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Maximum force occurs at 90° (perpendicular) because sin90° = 1.

blank:1.explanation: Parallel gives zero force; perpendicular gives maximum.
Antiparallel (180°) gives zero force; perpendicular (90°) gives maximum.

blank:2.explanation: At 0° the force is zero; maximum is at 90°.
At 180° the force is zero; maximum is at 90°.

toLevel2.question: Both parallel (0°) and {{blank:1}} (180°) orientations give {{blank:2}} magnetic force on the wire.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: At both 0° and 180°, sinθ = 0, so the magnetic force is zero in both cases.

blank:1.explanation: Perpendicular (90°) gives maximum force; antiparallel (180°) gives zero.
The specific term for 180° is antiparallel, not diagonal.

blank:2.explanation: Both 0° and 180° give zero force, not maximum.
Both orientations give exactly zero force.

toLevel3.question: Why does a parallel orientation of current and field produce zero magnetic force?
toLevel3.correct: The cross product of two parallel vectors is zero, meaning no perpendicular force component exists
toLevel3.correctExplanation: F = IL × B. When I and B are parallel, the cross product magnitude is |I||B|sinθ = 0. No force results.

distractors.answer: The magnetic field is cancelled by the current's own field when they are parallel to each other
distractors.explanation: The fields do not cancel; the cross product is zero because parallel vectors have no perpendicular component.

distractors.answer: The wire becomes invisible to the field when aligned parallel to its direction completely
distractors.explanation: The wire still interacts with the field; the geometry simply produces zero force.

distractors.answer: The current stops flowing when aligned with the field, removing the source of force entirely
distractors.explanation: Current continues to flow regardless of orientation; the force is zero due to the cross product.

toLevel3.question: How does the formula F = nIlBsinθ explain why parallel wires produce zero force?
toLevel3.correct: When θ = 0° or 180°, sinθ = 0, making the entire force expression equal to zero
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The sinθ factor directly accounts for the angle. At parallel orientations, sinθ = 0 regardless of how large the other quantities are.

distractors.answer: When θ = 0°, sinθ = 1, but the other factors happen to cancel each other out exactly
distractors.explanation: sin0° = 0, not 1; it is the sinθ term that makes the force zero.

distractors.answer: The formula F = nIlBsinθ does not apply to parallel cases; a different formula is needed
distractors.explanation: The formula applies at all angles; at parallel, it correctly gives zero.

distractors.answer: The sinθ term only affects direction, not magnitude, so the force is still non-zero at 0°
distractors.explanation: sinθ directly affects magnitude; sin0° = 0 means zero force magnitude.

toLevel3.question: A student incorrectly calculates a non-zero force for a wire parallel to the field. What conceptual error have they likely made?
toLevel3.correct: They forgot to include the sinθ factor and used F = nIlB instead of F = nIlBsinθ
toLevel3.correctExplanation: F = nIlB applies only when θ = 90°. For any other angle, sinθ must be included. At 0°, sinθ = 0 and the force is zero.

distractors.answer: They used the wrong value of current; the correct current would give zero force directly
distractors.explanation: The error is omitting sinθ, not using the wrong current value.

distractors.answer: They forgot to convert metres to centimetres before substituting into the formula given
distractors.explanation: The error is conceptual (missing sinθ), not a unit conversion issue.

distractors.answer: They used the correct formula and the force is genuinely non-zero for parallel orientation
distractors.explanation: The force is genuinely zero at parallel; the student's error is omitting sinθ.

toLevel3.question: In a DC motor, the sides of the coil that are parallel to the field contribute no force. Why does this matter for motor design?
toLevel3.correct: It means only the perpendicular sides create useful torque, reducing the effective force-producing length
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The top and bottom sides of a rectangular coil in a uniform field may be parallel to B, contributing zero force. Only the two perpendicular sides produce useful torque.

distractors.answer: It does not matter because all sides produce equal force regardless of orientation to the field
distractors.explanation: Parallel sides produce zero force; only perpendicular sides contribute.

distractors.answer: It means the motor cannot work because too many sides are parallel at any given moment
distractors.explanation: The perpendicular sides provide sufficient torque; the parallel sides just contribute nothing.

distractors.answer: It improves motor efficiency because the parallel sides save energy by not experiencing any force
distractors.explanation: The parallel sides are a design limitation, not an efficiency improvement.

toLevel3.question: Compare the force on a wire at 30° to the field versus a wire parallel to the field. What is the ratio of forces?
toLevel3.correct: The wire at 30° experiences sin30° = 0.5 of the maximum force; the parallel wire experiences zero
toLevel3.correctExplanation: At 30°: F = nIlBsin30° = 0.5nIlB. At 0°: F = nIlBsin0° = 0. The ratio is 0.5 to 0.

distractors.answer: Both wires experience the same force because the angle does not affect the force magnitude
distractors.explanation: The angle directly affects force through sinθ; 30° gives half maximum, 0° gives zero.

distractors.answer: The parallel wire has double the force because it aligns perfectly with the field direction
distractors.explanation: Alignment with the field means zero force, not double.

distractors.answer: The wire at 30° has zero force because it is not exactly perpendicular to the field direction
distractors.explanation: The force at 30° is non-zero (sin30° = 0.5); only exactly 0° or 180° gives zero.

toLevel3.question: Why is recognising the parallel case important for solving physics exam problems?
toLevel3.correct: It allows you to immediately identify zero-force situations without needing any calculation
toLevel3.correctExplanation: If you notice the current is parallel to the field, you can state the force is zero without calculating. This saves time and prevents errors.

distractors.answer: It is not important because exam questions never involve parallel orientations of current and field
distractors.explanation: Exam questions frequently test whether students recognise the zero-force parallel case.

distractors.answer: It is important only for gravitational force problems, not for magnetic force problems directly
distractors.explanation: The parallel case is specifically about magnetic force, not gravitational.

distractors.answer: Recognising it is useful only if the current is exactly zero, which rarely occurs in exams
distractors.explanation: The key is the angle being 0° or 180°, not the current being zero.

toLevel3.question: A wire at 180° (antiparallel) to the field experiences the same zero force as a wire at 0° (parallel).
toLevel3.correctExplanation: sin180° = 0 just like sin0° = 0. Both orientations give zero magnetic force.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Both sin0° and sin180° equal zero; the force is zero in both cases.

toLevel3.question: The force formula F = nIlBsinθ gives zero force when sinθ = {{blank:1}}, which occurs at θ = 0° and θ = {{blank:2}}°.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: sin0° = 0 and sin180° = 0. Both parallel and antiparallel orientations give zero force.

blank:1.explanation: sinθ = 1 at 90°, which gives maximum force, not zero.
sinθ = 0.5 at 30°, which gives half maximum; zero requires sinθ = 0.

blank:2.explanation: At 90°, sinθ = 1 (maximum force); zero occurs at 180°.
At 45°, sinθ ≈ 0.71 (non-zero force); zero occurs at 180°.

toLevel3.question: In a DC motor, only the coil sides that are {{blank:1}} to the field produce force; the sides that are {{blank:2}} contribute nothing.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The perpendicular sides experience maximum force (sin90° = 1), while the parallel sides experience zero force (sin0° = 0).

blank:1.explanation: Parallel sides produce zero force; perpendicular sides produce force.
Antiparallel gives zero force; perpendicular gives maximum.

blank:2.explanation: Perpendicular sides produce force; parallel sides contribute nothing.
Parallel sides specifically contribute zero force.

toLevel3.question: A wire carrying current northward in a northward field has {{blank:1}} force because the {{blank:2}} product of parallel vectors is zero.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The cross product I × B = 0 when I and B are parallel, resulting in zero magnetic force.

blank:1.explanation: Parallel orientation gives zero force, not maximum.
The force is zero when current and field are parallel.

blank:2.explanation: The dot product of parallel vectors is maximum; it is the cross product that is zero.
The relevant operation is the cross product, which gives zero for parallel vectors.

toLevel4.question: A rectangular coil in a uniform magnetic field has two sides perpendicular to the field and two sides parallel. Calculate the total useful force if n = 20, I = 3 A, l = 0.1 m (perpendicular side length), and B = 0.4 T.
toLevel4.correct: 4.8 N total (2.4 N on each perpendicular side; zero on parallel sides)
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Each perpendicular side: F = nIlB = 20 × 3 × 0.1 × 0.4 = 2.4 N. Two sides: 4.8 N total. Parallel sides contribute zero.

distractors.answer: 9.6 N because all four sides of the coil contribute equal force to the total
distractors.explanation: Only two sides are perpendicular and produce force; the parallel sides give zero.

distractors.answer: 2.4 N because only one side of the rectangular coil produces useful force
distractors.explanation: Both perpendicular sides produce 2.4 N each, giving 4.8 N total.

distractors.answer: 0 N because the forces on opposite sides cancel each other completely out
distractors.explanation: The forces on opposite sides are in opposite directions, creating torque, not cancelling the total.

toLevel4.question: A wire runs east to west, and the magnetic field points east. The wire carries current to the west. What is the force?
toLevel4.correct: Zero, because the current is antiparallel to the field (180°)
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Current is west and field is east — antiparallel (180°). sin180° = 0, so the force is zero.

distractors.answer: Maximum, because the current opposes the field with full strength in this case
distractors.explanation: Antiparallel gives sin180° = 0; the force is zero regardless of how strong the current or field is.

distractors.answer: Upward, determined by the right-hand slap rule for opposing current and field
distractors.explanation: The slap rule cannot give a direction when the force is zero; parallel and antiparallel give no force.

distractors.answer: Downward, because opposing the field direction always pushes the wire down toward earth
distractors.explanation: The force is zero because sin180° = 0.

toLevel4.question: A wire is initially perpendicular to a field and experiences a force of 2.0 N. It is then rotated to be parallel to the field. By how much does the force change?
toLevel4.correct: The force decreases by 2.0 N, from 2.0 N to zero
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Perpendicular gives the full force (2.0 N). Parallel gives zero. The change is a decrease of 2.0 N.

distractors.answer: The force stays at 2.0 N because rotating the wire does not affect the force magnitude
distractors.explanation: The force depends on the angle; rotating to parallel reduces it to zero.

distractors.answer: The force increases to 4.0 N because parallel alignment doubles the magnetic interaction
distractors.explanation: Parallel gives zero force, not double.

distractors.answer: The force changes to 1.0 N because it is halved when the wire is rotated 90 degrees
distractors.explanation: The force goes from maximum to zero, not from maximum to half.

toLevel4.question: In a galvanometer coil, at what angular position of the coil do the active sides become parallel to the field, and what happens to the torque?
toLevel4.correct: When the coil plane is perpendicular to the field, the active sides are parallel to B and the torque drops to zero
toLevel4.correctExplanation: When the coil plane is perpendicular to the field, the current in the active sides runs parallel to B, giving sin0° = 0 and zero torque.

distractors.answer: The torque is maximum when the sides are parallel because the lever arm is at its greatest
distractors.explanation: When sides are parallel to B, the force is zero regardless of the lever arm.

distractors.answer: The sides are never parallel to the field because the coil is always at an angle in practice
distractors.explanation: As the coil rotates, its sides pass through the parallel orientation, where torque is zero.

distractors.answer: The torque is constant at all positions because the field is uniform throughout the device
distractors.explanation: Uniform field does not prevent the torque from varying with angle; it drops to zero when sides are parallel.

toLevel4.question: A wire at 60° to the field experiences a force of 1.73 N. What force would it experience at 0° and at 90°?

distractors.answer: 1.73 N at both 0° and 90° because the force does not change with angle
distractors.explanation: The force varies with sinθ; it is zero at 0° and 2.0 N at 90°.

distractors.answer: 0 N at 0° and 1.73 N at 90° because 90° is the same force as 60° here
distractors.explanation: At 90°, sin90° = 1, giving 2.0 N, which is greater than the 1.73 N at 60°.

distractors.answer: 1.0 N at 0° and 3.46 N at 90° because the force doubles from 60° to 90°
distractors.explanation: At 0° the force is zero; at 90° it is 2.0 N (nIlB), not 3.46 N.

toLevel4.question: Why do curved pole pieces in a DC motor eliminate the zero-torque problem at the parallel position?
toLevel4.correct: They create a radial field so the active coil sides are always perpendicular to the field at every position
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Curved poles make the field radial, ensuring the current in the active sides is always perpendicular to the local field direction, maintaining non-zero torque.

distractors.answer: They increase the field strength to overcome the zero-force condition at parallel positions
distractors.explanation: Stronger field does not fix zero force at 0°; the radial geometry ensures perpendicularity.

distractors.answer: They reverse the current automatically at the parallel position to restore the lost force
distractors.explanation: Current reversal is done by the commutator; curved poles fix the angle, not the current.

distractors.answer: They block the field at the parallel position so the coil never reaches that orientation
distractors.explanation: Curved poles redirect the field radially; they do not block it.

toLevel4.question: A straight wire passes through a uniform magnetic field region. Part of the wire is perpendicular to B and part runs parallel to B. How do you calculate the total force?
toLevel4.correct: Only the perpendicular section contributes force; the parallel section has zero force and is ignored
toLevel4.correctExplanation: F = nIlBsinθ applies to each section. The parallel part has sinθ = 0 and contributes nothing. Only the perpendicular part's length is used.

distractors.answer: The total length of the wire is used because all sections experience force equally in the field
distractors.explanation: Only the perpendicular part produces force; the parallel part contributes zero.

distractors.answer: The parallel section produces more force because it is aligned with the field for maximum coupling
distractors.explanation: Parallel alignment produces zero force, not more force.

distractors.answer: The forces from both sections are averaged to find the total force on the entire wire
distractors.explanation: The forces are summed (not averaged), and the parallel section contributes zero.

toLevel4.question: At 60° to the field, the force is F = nIlBsin{{blank:1}}° ≈ {{blank:2}} × nIlB.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: sin60° ≈ 0.866 ≈ 0.87. The force at 60° is about 87% of the maximum perpendicular force.

blank:1.explanation: The angle to the field is 60°, not 30°.
The wire is at 60° to the field, not 90°.

blank:2.explanation: sin60° ≈ 0.87, not 0.50 (that is sin30°).
sin60° ≈ 0.87, not 1.00 (that is sin90°).

toLevel4.question: Curved pole pieces ensure the field is {{blank:1}}, so the active coil sides are always {{blank:2}} to the local field.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: A radial field points outward from the centre at every point, keeping the active coil sides perpendicular and maintaining constant torque.

blank:1.explanation: The key feature is radial direction, not just uniformity.
A radial field is the goal, not a parallel field.

blank:2.explanation: The coil sides must be perpendicular to the field for force; parallel gives zero.
Antiparallel gives zero force; perpendicular gives maximum.

toLevel4.question: For a wire at angle θ to B, the force varies as {{blank:1}}, reaching zero when θ equals {{blank:2}}° or 180°.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: F = nIlBsinθ. The force is zero when sinθ = 0, which occurs at θ = 0° (parallel) and θ = 180° (antiparallel).

blank:1.explanation: The force varies as sinθ, not cosθ.
The force varies as sinθ, not tanθ.

blank:2.explanation: At 90° sinθ = 1 (maximum); zero occurs at 0°.
At 45° sinθ ≈ 0.71 (non-zero); zero occurs at 0°.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why the cross product I × B = 0 when I is parallel to B, using the geometric interpretation of the cross product.
toLevel5.correct: The cross product magnitude equals |I||B|sinθ, and sin0° = 0, so no perpendicular component exists to create a force
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Geometrically, the cross product represents the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors. When parallel, the area is zero because the vectors lie along the same line.

distractors.answer: The cross product is maximum when vectors are parallel because they are fully aligned together
distractors.explanation: The cross product is zero when parallel; the dot product is maximum when parallel.

distractors.answer: The cross product is undefined for parallel vectors and cannot be calculated in those cases
distractors.explanation: The cross product is well-defined for all vectors; it simply equals zero when they are parallel.

distractors.answer: The cross product gives a scalar zero, meaning the force has zero magnitude but still a direction
distractors.explanation: A zero vector has no meaningful direction; the force is simply zero.

toLevel5.question: A student argues: 'Since the wire's own field still exists when current is parallel to the external field, there should still be a force.' Evaluate this argument.
toLevel5.correct: The wire's field exists, but the field interaction pattern is symmetric around the wire, producing no net force
toLevel5.correctExplanation: When the current is parallel to B, the wire's circular field interacts with the uniform external field symmetrically on all sides. The forces cancel, giving zero net force.

distractors.answer: The student is correct; the force is non-zero but too small to measure with standard equipment
distractors.explanation: The force is exactly zero by symmetry; it is not merely small.

distractors.answer: The wire's field disappears when aligned with the external field due to destructive interference
distractors.explanation: The wire's field does not disappear; it superimposes symmetrically, giving zero net force.

distractors.answer: The student is correct; there is always a force whenever a field exists around a current-carrying wire
distractors.explanation: The net force is zero due to symmetry; having a field does not guarantee a net force.

toLevel5.question: In a velocity selector, charged particles move parallel to an electric field but perpendicular to a magnetic field. Why is it crucial that the velocity is perpendicular to B?
toLevel5.correct: If the velocity were parallel to B, there would be no magnetic force, and the selector could not function
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The magnetic force F = qvBsinθ requires v ⊥ B (sinθ = 1) for maximum deflection. If v ∥ B, the magnetic force is zero and selection cannot occur.

distractors.answer: The velocity direction does not matter because the electric field handles all the selection work
distractors.explanation: Both fields are essential; the magnetic force must oppose the electric force for velocity selection.

distractors.answer: Parallel velocity would double the force, overwhelming the electric field's contribution entirely
distractors.explanation: Parallel velocity gives zero magnetic force, not double.

distractors.answer: Perpendicular velocity is preferred only for aesthetic symmetry in the device design blueprint
distractors.explanation: Perpendicularity is physically required for the magnetic force to exist.

toLevel5.question: Compare the torque on a motor coil when the coil plane is parallel to B versus when it is perpendicular to B.
toLevel5.correct: Torque is maximum when the coil plane is parallel to B (sides perpendicular to B) and zero when the plane is perpendicular to B (sides parallel to B)
toLevel5.correctExplanation: When the coil plane is parallel to B, the active sides are perpendicular to B, giving maximum force and torque. When the plane is perpendicular to B, the sides are parallel to B, giving zero force.

distractors.answer: Torque is constant regardless of the coil plane orientation in a uniform magnetic field always
distractors.explanation: Torque varies with the angle between the coil normal and B; it is not constant.

distractors.answer: Torque is maximum when the plane is perpendicular to B because the forces have maximum leverage
distractors.explanation: When the plane is perpendicular to B, the active sides are parallel to B and experience zero force.

distractors.answer: Torque is zero at all orientations because the forces on opposite sides always cancel each other
distractors.explanation: The forces create a couple (torque) when the sides are perpendicular to B.

toLevel5.question: A charged particle moves through a region where E and B fields are parallel to each other. The particle enters parallel to both fields. Analyse the forces acting on it.
toLevel5.correct: The electric force accelerates it along the field, but the magnetic force is zero because v is parallel to B
toLevel5.correctExplanation: F_E = qE acts along the field direction. F_B = qvBsinθ = 0 because θ = 0° (v parallel to B). Only the electric force acts.

distractors.answer: Both forces act on the particle equally, causing it to spiral through the combined field region
distractors.explanation: The magnetic force is zero when v is parallel to B; only the electric force acts.

distractors.answer: Neither force acts because the parallel fields cancel each other's effects on the particle
distractors.explanation: The electric force still acts; only the magnetic force is zero.

distractors.answer: The magnetic force is maximum because the particle moves along the strongest field direction
distractors.explanation: The magnetic force is zero when v is parallel to B; the angle matters, not the field strength.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate the statement: 'The sinθ dependence of magnetic force means that magnetic fields can never do work on charged particles.'
toLevel5.correct: This is true — the magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity, so it changes direction but not speed
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Since F is perpendicular to v (from the cross product), the force does zero work (W = F·d, and F ⊥ d). The particle's speed remains constant; only direction changes.

distractors.answer: This is false — magnetic fields can do work when the particle moves perpendicular to the field
distractors.explanation: Even when the particle moves perpendicular to B, the resulting force is perpendicular to v, doing no work.

distractors.answer: This is true only for parallel motion; perpendicular motion allows the magnetic field to do work
distractors.explanation: The force is always perpendicular to v regardless of the angle with B; no work is done.

distractors.answer: This is false — all forces do work when they cause displacement of the object they act upon
distractors.explanation: Only the component of force along the displacement does work; for magnetic force, this is always zero.

toLevel5.question: A wire is gradually rotated from 0° to 90° relative to a uniform magnetic field. Describe how the force varies during this rotation.
toLevel5.correct: The force increases from zero following a sine curve, reaching maximum at 90°
toLevel5.correctExplanation: F = nIlBsinθ. As θ increases from 0° to 90°, sinθ increases from 0 to 1, and the force follows the sine function.

distractors.answer: The force increases linearly from zero to maximum as the wire rotates through the 90 degrees
distractors.explanation: The force follows sinθ, which is not linear; it curves, increasing slowly at first then faster.

distractors.answer: The force stays at zero until 45° and then jumps to maximum at exactly 90 degrees instantly
distractors.explanation: The force increases continuously as sinθ increases; there is no sudden jump.

distractors.answer: The force decreases from maximum at 0° to zero at 90° following a cosine function curve
distractors.explanation: The force is zero at 0° and maximum at 90°; it increases with sinθ, not decreases.

toLevel5.question: In a tokamak fusion reactor, charged particles spiral around magnetic field lines. Analyse why the particles move freely along the field direction but are confined perpendicular to it.
toLevel5.correct: The magnetic force is zero for motion parallel to B (no confinement) but acts perpendicular to B (provides centripetal confinement)
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The parallel velocity component experiences zero force (v ∥ B gives sinθ = 0). The perpendicular component experiences a centripetal force (v ⊥ B gives sinθ = 1), confining the particle.

distractors.answer: The particles are confined in all directions equally by the strong magnetic field in the tokamak
distractors.explanation: Particles move freely along B; confinement is only perpendicular to the field lines.

distractors.answer: The parallel motion is stopped by collisions with the wall while the field confines perpendicularly
distractors.explanation: Particles must not hit walls; they move freely along B because the magnetic force is zero in that direction.

distractors.answer: The electric field confines along B while the magnetic field confines perpendicular to it simultaneously
distractors.explanation: The analysis concerns magnetic force only: zero along B and centripetal perpendicular to B.

toLevel5.question: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does {{blank:1}} work, changing the particle's {{blank:2}} but not its speed.
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Work = F·d requires a force component along the displacement. Since F ⊥ v, the work is zero; only direction changes.

blank:1.explanation: The magnetic force is perpendicular to displacement, doing zero work.
The work done by a magnetic force is exactly zero, not positive.

blank:2.explanation: The magnetic force changes direction, not speed; speed is unchanged because no work is done.
The magnetic force changes the particle's direction of motion, not its charge.

toLevel5.question: In a tokamak, particles spiral because the {{blank:1}} velocity component is confined by the magnetic force, while the {{blank:2}} component moves freely.
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The perpendicular velocity gives a centripetal magnetic force (confinement). The parallel velocity has zero magnetic force (free motion along the field).

blank:1.explanation: The parallel component moves freely; the perpendicular component is confined.
Only the perpendicular component is confined; the parallel component is free.

blank:2.explanation: The perpendicular component is confined; the parallel component moves freely.
The parallel component specifically moves freely along the field lines.
